constraints: The exchange uses proto3 binary messages.
Older workers remain deployed during the rollout.
For existing payouts, an absent memo has the same meaning as an empty memo.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: This works because an omitted memo is equivalent to the existing empty value. If absence later means “unknown” while empty means “intentionally blank,” the payload needs presence information instead of this default.
details.errorCorrection: Reusing a retired tag risks interpreting old payout bytes as memo data. Making the field mandatory rejects old-writer payloads, and deriving memo text from amount cannot recover text that was never stored.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Proto3 binary evolution can add a field without changing existing tags. The compatibility condition is semantic as well as syntactic: when an older writer omits the field, the new reader must apply a value that preserves the old record’s behavior.
details.scenarioApplication: The older payout workers keep reading the existing settlement fields and ignore the new memo tag. A new worker sees an empty memo for a record written before rollout, which the prompt says means exactly what it meant before.
details.transfer: When adding a serialized field, check both reader compatibility and the meaning of absence in old payloads; a new tag alone does not make a new default safe.

messages.text: The old binary tag remains in historical bytes; reusing it can make those bytes decode as the new memo.
Old writers omit it, so the new reader would reject records that the scenario requires it to keep settling.
Those facts do not encode memo text; deriving it invents information and changes old records.
A versioned message could route old workers, but the scenario already permits a fresh additive tag and compatible absent value; the extra message type does not solve a stated incompatibility.

feedback.reason: A new proto3 field has its own wire tag. Old binary readers ignore that unknown tag; new readers can parse old messages if absence maps to the already-defined empty-memo meaning.

options.text: Add the memo at a fresh tag, with absence retaining the existing empty-memo meaning.
Reuse the number of a deleted payout field because its old name is gone.
Require the memo before deploying any new reader.
Infer a missing memo from the payout amount and settled-order state.
Introduce a versioned payout message and route older workers through a compatibility adapter.

prompt: The payout record is exchanged as proto3 binary. Older workers must continue settling records written by the new service, and a missing memo must mean “no memo,” exactly as it does today. Which schema change keeps both readers meaningful?

constraints: Some messages omit `delay_minutes`.
Explicit zero clears a delay.
Omission means inherit the route value.
Keep the public `delay_minutes` field as a scalar; do not add a parallel presence field.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Presence is needed because this API assigns different meanings to absent and explicit zero. If zero and absence had identical semantics, implicit presence would be simpler and sufficient.
details.errorCorrection: A zero default erases the inherit case; a sentinel changes the allowed value contract; and a second boolean duplicates state that can become inconsistent with the minutes field.
details.mechanismOrProperty: With implicit presence, a scalar at its default does not reveal whether a sender omitted it or explicitly chose that value. Explicit presence records whether the field was supplied, independently of the scalar value.
details.scenarioApplication: A present `delay_minutes: 0` clears the delay. An absent field leaves the route’s inherited delay in force, matching the two meanings stated in the prompt.
details.transfer: When a serialized default value can be an explicit user choice, verify whether the format preserves field presence before using that default as a command.

messages.text: Implicit scalar presence cannot distinguish an explicitly set zero from an omitted field.
The existing payload contract gives omission the inherit meaning; inventing a sentinel changes the wire contract and constrains valid values.
That turns older omitted values into clear commands and loses the inherited route value.
A separate flag duplicates state that writers can desynchronize; explicit presence on the scalar represents the distinction directly.

feedback.reason: An implicit proto3 scalar collapses an omitted field and an explicitly supplied default into the same value. Explicit presence lets the reader tell “inherit” from “clear to zero.”

options.text: Keep an implicit-presence scalar and treat zero as the clear command.
Reserve `-1` to mean inherit and use zero for clear.
Set the schema default to zero and apply it whenever the field is absent.
Add and synchronize a separate `delay_was_set` flag beside the scalar.
Use scalar presence so omission inherits while an explicit zero clears the delay.

prompt: The transit update message has an integer `delay_minutes`. A dispatcher may explicitly set it to zero to clear a delay; an older message with no delay field means “use the route’s inherited value.” Which representation preserves that distinction?

constraints: Old serialized meter messages remain in archives.
They include field number 6 and the old name `legacy_peak`.
The field’s business meaning has been retired.
Archived ProtoJSON/TextFormat records also use the name `legacy_peak`.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: The reservation is needed because archives and possible text payloads outlive the active field. If neither number nor name had ever been serialized, this historical collision would not exist.
details.errorCorrection: Reserving only the name leaves the binary tag reusable. Keeping the field but relabeling its value is worse: it makes an old peak reading appear to record a new source fact.
details.mechanismOrProperty: A protobuf field number identifies a binary value; its name appears in textual representations such as ProtoJSON. Retiring both identifiers prevents either archived form from being read as a new field.
details.scenarioApplication: The archived binary records retain tag 6, and archived textual records name `legacy_peak`. Future schemas reserve the number and name so neither representation is reinterpreted as `peak_source`.
details.transfer: When a retired protobuf field exists in binary and textual archives, preserve each serialized identifier those formats use.

messages.text: Archived bytes still carry tag 6; a new field at that tag would decode old data as a different fact.
Name reservation protects textual forms, not the binary tag that identifies the archived value.
The old field’s retired meaning is not evidence for the new meaning; replay would silently relabel historical data.
The first message’s number remains available for accidental reuse; historical bytes still make that reuse unsafe.

feedback.reason: The binary archive uses tag 6 and the textual archive uses `legacy_peak`; retire both identifiers so neither old value is assigned a new meaning.

options.text: Assign number 6 to a new `peak_source` field and leave the old name unused.
Reserve `legacy_peak`, but give `peak_source` a new number and leave old tag 6 unreserved.
Keep the old field active and reinterpret its value as the new peak source.
Remove the field; reserve tag 6 and the `legacy_peak` name used by archived records.
Move new fields to a second message and leave number 6 available in the first.

prompt: Archived meter messages still contain field number 6 named `legacy_peak`. The field is no longer read, but old archives may be replayed and future code must not reinterpret those bytes. What should the schema change retain?

constraints: Clients consume ProtoJSON, not only binary messages.
They persist the exact key `captionErrorCode`.
The field’s value and wire number are unchanged.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: This preserves the JSON contract because clients persist that exact key. If consumers could migrate together, the service could instead coordinate a deliberate JSON-name change.
details.errorCorrection: A plain proto rename changes the default JSON key. A new tag is unrelated to JSON naming and breaks an identity the prompt explicitly preserves; duplicated fields create competing values.
details.mechanismOrProperty: ProtoJSON uses lowerCamelCase derived from the proto field name unless the schema provides an explicit `json_name`. Its parser accepts the configured JSON name and the original proto name, so the producer can rename its source field while retaining the required external key.
details.scenarioApplication: The renamed field still prints as `captionErrorCode`; existing clients find the persisted property, and the unchanged tag continues to identify the same value in binary messages.
details.transfer: For protobuf-backed JSON APIs, evaluate field numbers and JSON property names separately; binary compatibility does not guarantee JSON compatibility.

messages.text: The default JSON key follows the new proto name, so stored clients looking for `captionErrorCode` will miss the value.
ProtoJSON keys use field names, not field numbers; changing the tag would also unnecessarily break binary compatibility.
Two writable copies can disagree and make the consumer choose between conflicting values; this is a name-mapping problem, not two facts.
The scenario says clients cannot be updated, and it moves schema evolution work onto consumers that do not recognize the new key.

feedback.reason: ProtoJSON normally derives its key from the proto field name, but the `json_name` option supplies a stable external name. Because the field number is unchanged, the binary identity can remain unchanged too.

options.text: Rename the proto field and rely on the default JSON-name conversion.
Keep the new field name but change its number to signal a new revision.
Declare `json_name: "captionErrorCode"` on the renamed proto field.
Keep two independent fields and write the error code to both.
Leave the schema as-is and require old clients to check both JSON spellings.

prompt: Caption clients store ProtoJSON with the key `captionErrorCode`. The proto field is being renamed internally to `provider_error_code`; clients cannot be updated in this release. What keeps the JSON property stable while the binary tag remains unchanged?

constraints: Older messages omit `RewardState`.
An omitted state must not authorize a grant.
The enum is proto3 and its first declared value is the default.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: This prevents default from granting because the scenario distinguishes “no decision” from “eligible.” If the old default already meant eligible, a zero sentinel would change the application contract and needs a migration plan.
details.errorCorrection: Making eligibility zero turns every older message into an apparent grant. An arbitrary unknown number does not change which value the runtime supplies for an omitted field.
details.mechanismOrProperty: A proto3 enum’s first value must have numeric value zero and is returned when an implicit-presence field is absent. Naming that value `UNSPECIFIED` makes the legacy/default state visible to callers.
details.scenarioApplication: A campaign message written before `RewardState` existed decodes to `UNSPECIFIED`; only a message carrying an explicit eligible state can satisfy the grant check.
details.transfer: For enum fields added to evolving messages, choose the zero value by examining what old omitted payloads should mean, not by selecting the most common active state.

messages.text: Omission returns the first enum value, so old messages would look eligible despite carrying no grant decision.
An undeclared number does not change the zero value returned for an omitted enum field.
An absent proto3 string reads as empty, which would still authorize the action and encode the opposite of the required safety boundary.
That preserves the unsafe default behavior rather than distinguishing an old omitted field from an explicit decision.

feedback.reason: For proto3 enums, the first declared value is the default when a message omits the field. A zero-valued unspecified state prevents absence from impersonating an authorization.

options.text: Make `REWARD_STATE_ELIGIBLE = 0` the first value so old messages stay concise.
Declare `UNSPECIFIED = 0` and grant only when the message explicitly says eligible.
Use an undeclared number as a no-decision marker, then translate it before granting.
Change the enum field to a string whose empty value means eligible.
Keep `ELIGIBLE = 0` and add a caller check that grants on the default.

prompt: Campaign reward messages gain an enum `RewardState`. Older messages omit the field, and the reader must not treat an omitted state as “eligible to grant.” Which enum layout makes the absent value explicit and safe?

constraints: Snapshots from three formats remain stored.
Each format has a known decoder/migration path.
A restore must not guess the format from whichever fields happen to be present.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A version field is useful here because multiple durable formats coexist and each has a known decoder. A format that is never stored beyond one coordinated deployment may not need this historical dispatch.
details.errorCorrection: Field-shape inference confuses absence with an older format, while parsing all records as latest risks assigning today’s defaults to yesterday’s data.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Stored bytes do not identify their schema reliably when fields may be optional or absent. A version discriminator makes the decoding path explicit and allows each historical format to have a deliberate migration step.
details.scenarioApplication: The snapshot envelope says 1, 2, or 3; the loader selects the matching decoder, then performs the known migration before exposing the route to the editor.
details.transfer: When persisted representations span schema generations, record their format identity and make the migration chain explicit instead of guessing from a partial payload.

messages.text: A later format may omit an optional field, so shape inspection can confuse a valid newer snapshot with an older one.
A default can invent current semantics for old data and cannot replace transformations needed between format generations.
The identifier selects a record, not its serialization format; absent version metadata still leaves the decoder ambiguous.
The scenario requires restoring all retained generations; rewriting archives is a separate migration and is not needed to identify their format.

feedback.reason: An explicit version tells the loader which historical shape it is reading. A matching decoder can then apply only the transformations defined for that version.

options.text: Persist a format version, then select that format’s decoder or migration.
Guess the decoder from whichever optional fields happen to be present.
Parse every snapshot directly with the newest model and fill missing fields with current defaults.
Split snapshots into unversioned tables and select a table from the snapshot ID.
Rewrite every archived snapshot into version 3 before allowing restore.

prompt: Map-editor snapshots from three schema generations are still stored. Version 1 used `line`, version 2 introduced `route`, and version 3 adds review metadata. Restoring a snapshot must use the decoder for the format that wrote it. What should the envelope provide?

constraints: Messages remain protobuf binary end to end.
The relay uses the same parsed message object for reserialization.
No JSON conversion or field-by-field reconstruction occurs.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: This relies on the scenario’s binary, message-oriented relay. A JSON intermediary or field-by-field mapping needs a different contract because it cannot rely on this unknown-field retention path.
details.errorCorrection: A ProtoJSON round trip has no unknown-field representation, and creating a new message from only known accessors omits the unrecognized tag. Rejecting or clearing it also defeats the stated relay behavior.
details.mechanismOrProperty: An older parser stores an unrecognized protobuf field as unknown data. The proto3 binary message serializer includes that unknown data when serializing the same message object.
details.scenarioApplication: The old campaign relay never needs to understand `season_id`; it forwards the parsed message as binary, leaving the new field available to the downstream new reader.
details.transfer: When an older protobuf intermediary must forward fields it cannot interpret, preserve the message object in binary form instead of translating it through a lossy representation.

messages.text: ProtoJSON does not carry unknown fields, so the relay would drop `season_id` before the downstream reader sees it.
The old schema has no `season_id` field to copy; rebuilding from known fields discards the unknown bytes.
The relay is specified to pass messages it does not interpret; rejecting the new tag prevents a compatible downstream consumer from receiving it.
That deliberately removes the only representation of `season_id` available to this old relay.

feedback.reason: Proto3 messages preserve unknown fields when the same message is parsed and serialized in binary form. JSON conversion or reconstruction from known fields can discard them.

options.text: Round-trip through ProtoJSON before relaying the message.
Rebuild a message from only fields known to the relay.
Reject any message containing a field unknown to the relay.
Drop unknown fields before serialization.
Reserialize the same parsed message object so unknown fields remain intact.

prompt: The campaign service relays proto3 binary messages between a newer reward producer and an older consumer. The relay parses and reserializes the same generated message object; it does not convert to JSON or copy fields into a new object. The new producer adds `season_id`. Which relay behavior preserves that field for a downstream new reader?

constraints: Scan order is meaningful.
Duplicate station codes are valid.
The serialized payload must retain every scan event.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A map is suitable if each station has one current value and ordering is irrelevant. The prompt instead requires an ordered history with repeated station codes.
details.errorCorrection: A station-keyed map merges duplicate scans. Sorting by station code or retaining only a latest timestamp replaces event order with a different ordering or loses events.
details.mechanismOrProperty: The repeated-field contract is a sequence: each element remains present and its order is preserved. A map is a key/value collection, so duplicate keys cannot represent two separate scans and its iteration order is not the event sequence.
details.scenarioApplication: The two scans at the same station remain two elements in their original positions, so the receiver can render the actual hand-off order.
details.transfer: Choose a serialized collection by the information the consumer needs to recover: a sequence preserves order and duplicates; a map models unique-key lookup.

messages.text: A map collapses duplicate keys and does not preserve the event sequence required by the receiver.
Station order is not scan order; sorting cannot recover the original order after entries are keyed by station.
The count indicates multiplicity but cannot reconstruct the distinct event values or their order.
Multiple scans at one station and equal timestamps leave no complete order to infer from the reduced data.

feedback.reason: A repeated protobuf field preserves element order. A map represents unique keys and may reorder entries or drop duplicate-key values.

options.text: Store the last scan for each station code in a map.
Use a map and sort entries by station code when reading.
Store one entry per station plus a count of repeated scans.
Keep the scans in an ordered repeated message field.
Store only the latest timestamp per station and infer the sequence later.

prompt: The logistics hand-off record contains repeated scan events. The receiver must display them in scan order, and two scans may share the same station code. Which field shape preserves both facts?

constraints: The field is a protobuf `int64`.
Values may exceed JavaScript’s exact integer range.
The receiver must echo the same identifier without rounding.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: This choice follows ProtoJSON’s mapping for int64 and the client’s stated precision limit. A client with an exact 64-bit integer type could use that type internally after parsing the string.
details.errorCorrection: Parsing the value as Number rounds some large identifiers. Narrowing to int32 rejects valid IDs, while splitting or floating-point formatting adds lossy conversions.
details.mechanismOrProperty: A JavaScript Number cannot exactly represent every integer above its safe-integer limit. ProtoJSON’s default string representation for int64 keeps the decimal digits exact until the client chooses an integer-safe representation.
details.scenarioApplication: The ledger emits the full reference as a JSON string; the client stores and echoes those digits without converting them through floating-point arithmetic.
details.transfer: For 64-bit identifiers crossing JSON into runtimes with floating-point numbers, preserve the value as a decimal string or use an exact integer parser.

messages.text: Values above the stated exact-integer range can be rounded, so an echoed reference may identify another repayment.
The valid references exceed that range; narrowing the field loses identifiers rather than preserving them.
A floating-point conversion can lose integer precision before it is placed in the string.
That invents a multi-field convention and parser burden when the existing ProtoJSON mapping already represents int64 values as strings.

feedback.reason: ProtoJSON represents 64-bit integers as strings by default to avoid precision loss in consumers that use IEEE-754 numbers, including JavaScript Number.

options.text: Convert the int64 to a JavaScript number and echo that number.
Change the field to `int32` to make every JSON client represent it exactly.
Keep the `int64` field and represent it as a decimal string in ProtoJSON for JavaScript.
Serialize the reference as a floating-point decimal string and round on receipt.
Split the identifier into numeric chunks and recombine them at the receiver.

prompt: A lending ledger sends a 64-bit repayment reference through ProtoJSON to a JavaScript client. Some references are larger than 9,007,199,254,740,991, and the client must echo the exact identifier. Which representation should the JSON contract use?

constraints: The digest is compared across different protobuf implementations.
The logical message may contain repeated values and unknown fields.
The signature must identify the logical record, not one encoder’s byte layout.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Canonicalization is warranted because the signature is compared across implementations and versions. If the digest were only an opaque checksum stored beside one exact byte sequence, hashing those stored bytes could be sufficient.
details.errorCorrection: A deterministic option can stabilize one serializer’s output without making a universal cross-version canonical standard. Raw JSON and local known-field views have their own ordering or omission differences.
details.mechanismOrProperty: A cryptographic digest compares bytes, not abstract messages. Protobuf serialization can vary in field order and unknown-field handling, so an application requiring stable cross-implementation bytes must define which logical fields and ordering enter the signature.
details.scenarioApplication: The tournament service first builds the agreed versioned signing projection, including the record’s defined repeated values and unknown-data policy, then hashes that canonical representation.
details.transfer: When signatures or content IDs must survive serializer changes, specify a canonical logical projection instead of treating a protocol’s ordinary bytes as canonical.

messages.text: Protobuf serialization is not canonical; equivalent messages can have different byte encodings across versions or implementations.
Deterministic output is not a guarantee of a universal canonical encoding across all implementations and future versions.
Different schema versions may then sign different logical content, and dropping unknown data can omit fields that belong to the record.
JSON field ordering and formatting can differ; raw text is not the canonical logical representation specified by the contract.

feedback.reason: Protocol Buffers explicitly does not guarantee canonical serialization. A cross-implementation signature therefore needs an application-defined canonical representation for the logical data.

options.text: Hash each implementation’s ordinary protobuf serialization.
Sign a canonical, versioned projection of the logical message rather than encoder bytes.
Rely on deterministic protobuf output as the permanent cross-version signing format.
Hash only fields known to the local schema.
Hash whichever ProtoJSON text each implementation emits.

prompt: Tournament records are signed by a digest that must be identical when two supported protobuf implementations serialize the same logical message. The contract includes repeated values and unknown fields. Which signing input is dependable?

constraints: Stored ProtoJSON contains enum names as strings.
Both names represent the same numeric enum value during rollout.
Old serialized payloads remain readable until migration finishes.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: This staged alias process is useful because stored JSON outlives one release. If only binary protobuf data existed, numeric values—not enum spelling—would determine this particular compatibility issue.
details.errorCorrection: An in-place rename leaves existing JSON with a name the new schema may not recognize. Reusing the numeric value without the old alias does not preserve the old string; inventing a second value changes state semantics.
details.mechanismOrProperty: ProtoJSON uses enum names in its string representation. With aliases for one numeric value, parsers accept both names and serializers emit the first listed alias; changing alias order can therefore change output only after parsers know both.
details.scenarioApplication: The first rollout accepts both `AWAITING_REVIEW` and `PENDING_REVIEW` but still emits the old spelling. After the compatible parser is deployed, the schema order switches; the old name stays until persisted old payloads are no longer needed.
details.transfer: For enum renames in JSON protocols, plan parser acceptance before changing emitted names, and retire old spellings only when old serialized data is out of scope.

messages.text: Existing JSON stores the old enum name, so a parser without that name can reject those records.
ProtoJSON serializes enum names; equal numeric values do not make a deleted string name parseable.
This silently changes a historical refund state instead of preserving the meaning carried by the old name.
The prompt says the names represent one state; splitting them creates a second business state and complicates comparisons.

feedback.reason: ProtoJSON stores enum value names. The documented alias rollout lets parsers accept both names while serializers continue emitting the name listed first, so the emission switch can follow parser deployment.

options.text: Keep both names readable through migration; switch output after dual-name readers ship.
Replace `AWAITING_REVIEW` with `PENDING_REVIEW` in one schema release.
Keep the same numeric value but delete the old enum spelling.
Map unrecognized enum strings to the first enum value.
Give the new name a different number and treat it as a separate refund state.

prompt: The returns API persists ProtoJSON refund states. Existing payloads contain the enum string `AWAITING_REVIEW`; the internal name is changing to `PENDING_REVIEW`, and old stored payloads must still parse during a staged rollout. Which migration preserves that contract?

constraints: Inputs and analysis-code revisions are immutable.
Reviewers need to identify the exact pair used for the result.
The scenario does not require schema evolution.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Because the prompt guarantees immutable revisions and asks only for provenance, identifiers are enough; it does not justify an extra schema-version policy.
details.errorCorrection: Adding a schema migration layer does not supply provenance. Copying current sources or inferring from time can select content that differs from the revisions actually used.
details.mechanismOrProperty: A reproducible result needs stable identifiers for every immutable input that influenced it. Display names and timestamps are descriptive, but they do not select one exact dataset and code revision.
details.scenarioApplication: The published record stores both revision identifiers beside the result. A reviewer can retrieve that same pair instead of resolving each name to its latest version.
details.transfer: For snapshots that must be reproducible, persist the identity of each immutable input and executable dependency rather than a mutable label or timestamp.

messages.text: A name can resolve to a newer revision, so the rerun would not identify the inputs used by the published result.
Schema migration does not identify the immutable inputs or code that produced this result; the prompt expressly has no schema change.
Current copies may differ from the immutable revisions used at the time the result was produced.
A timestamp does not uniquely identify the dataset and code revisions if either can change independently.

feedback.reason: The requirement is provenance, not schema evolution: the result’s serialized snapshot must point to the exact immutable input and code revisions used to produce it.

options.text: Store display names and resolve the latest revisions when rerunning.
Add a schema version even though the stored result shape is unchanged.
Copy the current dataset and executable into the result after publication.
Record the publication timestamp and infer which revisions were current then.
Store immutable dataset and code revision IDs with the published result snapshot.

prompt: The notebook publishes a result together with the exact input dataset revision and analysis-code revision that produced it. Those revisions are immutable, and reviewers later rerun the same result. No schema change or old-reader migration is requested. What should the serialized snapshot retain?

constraints: `reviewer_note` supports explicit presence.
Absent and empty have different application meanings.
The consumer reads ProtoJSON.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: This depends on a presence-aware field and the API’s two stated meanings. With an implicit scalar where presence is unavailable, a separate operation or explicit wrapper would be needed to express the distinction.
details.errorCorrection: Omitting all empty strings deletes the clear command, while always emitting empty turns absence into clear. Null is defined as unset, and a text sentinel can be legitimate user data.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Presence-aware serialization carries both the field value and whether the field was set. ProtoJSON emits present values, including defaults; absent fields are omitted, and JSON null leaves ordinary fields unset.
details.scenarioApplication: The explicit empty reviewer note is emitted as `"reviewerNote": ""`, signaling clear. A record with no supplied note omits the key and retains the distinct “not supplied” state.
details.transfer: When a JSON update distinguishes absent from explicit default, preserve field presence; do not normalize both states to the same output.

messages.text: That erases an explicit clear and makes it indistinguishable from a request that supplied no note.
A receiver then interprets every older or untouched record as an explicit clear.
ProtoJSON parses null as unset for ordinary fields, so it does not preserve the requested clear distinction.
That changes user content into protocol control data and can collide with a legitimate note.

feedback.reason: For fields with presence, ProtoJSON emits a field only when it is present. An explicitly present empty value is therefore distinct from an absent field; null is parsed as unset.

options.text: Omit empty strings so the JSON payload stays compact.
Emit an empty string for every absent note.
Encode an explicit clear as JSON `null`.
Preserve presence: absent is unchanged; present-empty is clear.
Write a reserved phrase such as `[CLEAR]` into the note string.

prompt: The inspection JSON has a presence-aware `reviewer_note`. An absent note means “no note was supplied”; an explicitly present empty string means “clear the prior note.” How should the publisher serialize these two states?

constraints: Omission means no change.
An explicit clear is a separate operation.
ProtoJSON null is treated as an unset field.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A separate clear operation is warranted because the API assigns distinct meanings to omission and deletion. If the endpoint instead defined null as clear, that protocol could use null consistently.
details.errorCorrection: Null follows the endpoint’s stated unset semantics. Empty string is still a value, and an unrelated audit comment is not a reliable update command.
details.mechanismOrProperty: A partial-update protocol must encode whether a field was not mentioned, assigned a value, or explicitly cleared. In this endpoint, null collapses to unset, so the clear action needs its own operation marker or field-mask meaning.
details.scenarioApplication: The client omits `inspection_note` for no change, sends a value to replace it, and marks the field in the explicit clear operation when removal is intended.
details.transfer: For partial updates, enumerate no-op, set, and clear states before choosing JSON presence, null, wrappers, or a field mask.

messages.text: The endpoint’s ProtoJSON behavior treats null as unset, so it cannot mean clear in this contract.
Those two meanings collide; the receiver cannot tell a blank note from a clear request.
That makes “leave unchanged” look like an instruction to overwrite with the default.
Audit text does not encode the requested mutation and may be present for an ordinary update.

feedback.reason: A partial update needs three states here: absent/no-op, set to a value, and clear. ProtoJSON null does not represent the third state because it is parsed as unset.

options.text: Send `inspectionNote: null` to clear the stored note.
Treat empty as clear, including when it means explicitly blank.
Use a distinct clear operation; omission remains no change.
Send the empty default whenever the client has no update.
Infer a clear from the presence of a separate audit comment.

prompt: The mobile inspection endpoint uses ProtoJSON for partial updates. For `inspection_note`, omission means “leave the stored note unchanged,” but an explicit clear must remove it. The endpoint currently treats JSON null as unset. Which request shape can express both operations without overloading null?

constraints: Each issued payload is immutable after transmission.
A corrected issue references the rejected issue.
Auditors can request either historical issue.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: This version chain is needed because the prompt grants auditors access to either transmitted issue. A draft that was never sent could be edited in place if no reader depends on its prior form.
details.errorCorrection: Overwriting or keeping only the latest issue destroys the historical payload. Rebuilding the old issue from the current invoice assumes the original fields still exist unchanged.
details.mechanismOrProperty: When serialized exchange records are immutable, a correction creates a new version while preserving the old bytes and their identity. A predecessor link lets readers follow the issue chain without rewriting history.
details.scenarioApplication: The rejected issue remains available exactly as transmitted; the new issue stores the corrected fields and references the rejected record that it replaces.
details.transfer: For externally transmitted records that may be corrected, keep each sent representation immutable and link the new version to the one it supersedes.

messages.text: The original transmitted issue disappears, so an auditor cannot recover what the counterparty received.
A latest-only row cannot provide the exact earlier payload when an auditor requests the rejected issue.
The corrected fields may overwrite original values, so the original serialized message cannot be reconstructed reliably.
Both payloads remain, but the exchange no longer states which issue the correction supersedes.

feedback.reason: An immutable transmitted message should remain addressable as sent. A corrected issue is a new payload with a predecessor reference, not a mutation of the old serialization.

options.text: Replace the rejected record’s payload with the corrected fields.
Append a new immutable issue and link it to the rejected issue.
Store one invoice row and retain only the latest issue number.
Rebuild the rejected issue from current invoice fields and the correction note.
Append the corrected issue without its predecessor link.

prompt: An invoice issue is serialized as an immutable exchange record. A corrected invoice must point to the rejected issue, and auditors may later read either issue exactly as it was sent. Which persistence shape preserves that history?

constraints: Each policy revision is immutable and addressable.
The audit needs the exact policy used for the decision.
A user’s current policy can differ from the historical one.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: This is sufficient because the scenario guarantees immutable addressable policy revisions. If revisions could be deleted, retention would also need to keep the referenced revision available.
details.errorCorrection: Current state and a display name can resolve to a different or ambiguous policy. A timestamp is only a proxy for identity, and copying rules without their revision breaks the link to the published contract.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Versioned references preserve provenance: the decision points to one immutable policy revision, so later policy updates cannot change the audit interpretation.
details.scenarioApplication: The record stores both the allow/deny result and the policy revision identifier. An auditor loads that revision even if the badge or current policy has since changed.
details.transfer: When an outcome must be explained under historical rules, serialize the exact immutable rule-set identity used to decide it.

messages.text: That reconstructs today’s access state, not the revision that the original door decision evaluated.

feedback.reason: An audit record needs a stable identity for the exact immutable policy used, rather than a mutable badge state or display label.

constraints: The job may outlive a carrier outage.
The shipment address may change while the job waits.
The job must use the address revision approved at enqueue time.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: This applies because the prompt binds the job to enqueue-time approval. If the requirement were “always use the latest approved address,” latest-state lookup would be appropriate.
details.errorCorrection: A latest-state lookup can silently substitute a later address, while display text may be incomplete. Replacing the queued job discards the accepted revision, and timestamp inference may select an ambiguous edit.
details.mechanismOrProperty: A delayed operation needs a stable input snapshot when its contract is tied to a particular approval event. Storing an immutable revision reference makes replay independent of later updates.
details.scenarioApplication: The job records revision R at enqueue time. When the carrier recovers, the renderer loads R and prints the address that was approved for that job.
details.transfer: For retried jobs, serialize the identity of any mutable input whose value is fixed by the request or approval that created the job.

prompt: A shipping label may be queued before a carrier outage and printed after it. The approved shipment address can be corrected while the job waits; the queued job must print the revision that was approved when it was created. What should the serialized job carry?

constraints: Legacy payloads omit the window field.
For those records, omission means use the published room default.
New records may explicitly choose a different window.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: The default is safe because the prompt fixes the legacy meaning and says it has not changed for these records. If defaults evolve, old records need a versioned/default snapshot to preserve that meaning.
details.errorCorrection: Rewriting all records from today’s default can change history; zero-as-absent erases an explicit choice; rejecting omission contradicts the legacy contract.
details.mechanismOrProperty: A reader applies a default to an absent field only when that default matches the historical meaning of absence. Explicit values remain data; treating them as missing overwrites sender intent.
details.scenarioApplication: An old booking with no window uses its published room default. A new booking that stores a different window keeps that explicit value when read.
details.transfer: When reading older payloads, distinguish a documented absent-field default from a present value; do not apply today’s default blindly to all historical data.

messages.text: A later default change would alter old bookings that the prompt says retain their original default meaning.

This ignores the explicit historical default contract and can change how older bookings are handled.

feedback.reason: Defaults are part of the serialized contract: old omission has a stated meaning, while a present value is an explicit choice and must not be replaced.

options.text: Rewrite old records using today’s room default.

prompt: Legacy rehearsal records omit `cancellation_window_minutes`. Their original meaning is “use the room’s published default,” and the default has not changed for those records. New records may explicitly select another window. Which read rule preserves old and new meanings?
